**Cedar Springs** is a city in Kent County in the U.S. state of Michigan. The population was 3,627 at the 2020 census.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-5) Cedar Springs is a northern city of the Grand Rapids metropolitan area and is about 20 miles (32.2 km) north of Grand Rapids.

### Founding and early settlement
[edit]
The area that became Cedar Springs, named for the abundance of cedar trees and natural springs found throughout the vicinity, was settled in the mid-1850s, with early accounts noting pioneers such as Nicholas R. "N. R." Hill and Benjamin Fairchild arriving around 1855.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-everett1878-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-cityhistory-7) On February 4, 1857, the community's first post office was established, with Hill serving as its inaugural postmaster, a position he held into the 1880s.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-everett1878-6) In addition to establishing local postal service, Hill served in local civic capacities, including School Inspector and Justice of the Peace, and later represented the area in the Michigan Legislature.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-everett1878-6)
Platted beginning in 1859, the settlement straddled the boundary between Nelson Township to the east and Solon Township to the west.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-cityhistory-7) Hill owned and platted the eastern portion in Nelson Township, while co-founder Benjamin Fairchild, referred to in early Kent County histories as the "other father" of Cedar Springs, owned and platted the western side in Solon Township.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-everett1878-6) Together, Hill and Fairchild drained the surrounding cedar swamp and offered alternate village lots free of charge to newcomers willing to build on them, helping transform the remote outpost into a lumber and shingle-milling center.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-everett1878-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-cityhistory-7)

### Railroad development and village incorporation
[edit]
Growth accelerated in 1868 when the Grand Rapids and Indiana Railroad constructed a railway line through the community.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-cityhistory-7) Fairchild also actively promoted competing rail connections, serving as a director for the Muskegon and Greenville Railroad in 1870, an effort that early county historians noted ultimately cost him his personal fortune.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-everett1878-6)
In March 1871, the Michigan Legislature officially incorporated Cedar Springs as a village.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-cityhistory-7) The village's first charter election was held at Fairchild's residence on April 2, 1871, where voters elected him as Cedar Springs' first village president.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-everett1878-6)

### 20th century and Red Flannel heritage
[edit]
During its timber era, local merchants supplied red flannel undergarments to lumberjacks working through Michigan winters.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-cityhistory2-8) In 1936, amid the Great Depression, a New York newspaper writer remarked that red flannel underwear was no longer available in the United States; editors Grace Hamilton and Nina Babcock of the local _Cedar Springs Clipper_ responded in print that town merchant Jack Pollock had plenty of red flannels in stock.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-rffhistory2-9) Picked up by the Associated Press, the story sparked a wave of mail orders from across the country and abroad; ultimately bringing tens of thousands of orders to local merchants and helping sustain the village's economy through the final years of the Depression.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-rffhistory2-9)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-cityhistory2-8) To celebrate the publicity and resulting economic boost, residents held the first annual Red Flannel Day on November 11, 1939, cementing Cedar Springs' nickname as "The Red Flannel Town".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-rffhistory2-9) The Red Flannel Festival is held on the first Saturday of October to this very day.
In October 1959, Cedar Springs incorporated as a city, driven largely by the need to establish independent water distribution and sanitary sewer systems rather than remaining divided between the taxing jurisdictions of Nelson and Solon townships.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-cityhistory-7)

Cedar Springs is located just 20 minutes north of Michigan’s second largest city, Grand Rapids. Situated in northern Kent County, Cedar Springs covers about 2.1 square miles and has a population of 3,509. The community was named for the fine springs bordered by a grove of Cedar trees. Less than a mile from US 131, Cedar Springs provides easy access to the cultural amenities of the greater Grand Rapids area. Cedar Springs is an attractive community with tree-lined streets and a varied housing base. Taxes in Cedar Springs have remained steady with the City millage rate of 15.0642.
Cedar Springs has a small retail business district and a stable industrial base. The community has vast possibilities for future growth. Significant industry and business have been attracted to the Cedar Springs area, including Display Pack and various precision tool and die companies.
Cedar Springs is part of the Cedar Springs Public School district, which encompasses 110 square miles and is comprised of the City of Cedar Springs and 7 surrounding townships. Cedar Springs Public Schools are located on a single 100 acre campus near downtown Cedar Springs. The school system has recently completed a $27 million building and renovation project.
The Cedar Springs Area Parks and Recreation Board is actively exploring new means to provide programs for youth and adults. The annual Red Flannel Festival was first celebrated in 1939, making it one of the oldest festivals in Michigan. Red Flannel Day takes place on the first Saturday in October to celebrate the famous “drop seat” red long johns and red flannel nightwear.
Overall, Cedar Springs is a desirable residential community with its own identity and charm. The City has all of the benefits of a small community, while simultaneously offering big city amenities.

### High Quality of Life Throughout the County
Kent County is the fourth largest population center in Michigan. Covering 856 square miles, the County is home to 596,666 people. The County is composed of 21 townships, five villages and nine cities.
The greater Grand Rapids area forms the urban center of the County. Grand Rapids is known as the home of the 38th President of the United States, Gerald R. Ford. The Gerald R. Ford Museum is located in the City of Grand Rapids and the Gerald R. Ford International Airport is located within Kent County.
Kent County is the economic and manufacturing center of West Michigan. Major employers include Spectrum Health, Meijer Incorporated, Steelcase Incorporated, Alticor Incorporated and Spartan Stores. It is also the home of the Frederik Meijer Gardens, a significant cultural landmark of the Midwest.
Kent County offers a thriving arts community and a diverse range of entertainment options for every season. The County has over 50 parks, offering activities such as golfing, swimming, biking, roller blading, walking, cross country skiing, fishing, boating, camping and a variety of playing fields. The award-winning 12,000 seat Van Andel Arena, located in Grand Rapids, is home to the Griffins hockey team and the Rampage arena football team, as well as major concerts and sporting events. The Michigan White Caps call Fifth Third Ballpark their home. All of these venues are located within an easy 15-20 minute drive from Cedar Springs.

**Cedar Springs** is a city in Kent County in the U.S. state of Michigan. The population was 3,627 at the 2020 census.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-5) Cedar Springs is a northern city of the Grand Rapids metropolitan area and is about 20 miles (32.2 km) north of Grand Rapids.

### Founding and early settlement
[edit]
The area that became Cedar Springs, named for the abundance of cedar trees and natural springs found throughout the vicinity, was settled in the mid-1850s, with early accounts noting pioneers such as Nicholas R. "N. R." Hill and Benjamin Fairchild arriving around 1855.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-everett1878-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-cityhistory-7) On February 4, 1857, the community's first post office was established, with Hill serving as its inaugural postmaster, a position he held into the 1880s.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-everett1878-6) In addition to establishing local postal service, Hill served in local civic capacities, including School Inspector and Justice of the Peace, and later represented the area in the Michigan Legislature.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-everett1878-6)
Platted beginning in 1859, the settlement straddled the boundary between Nelson Township to the east and Solon Township to the west.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-cityhistory-7) Hill owned and platted the eastern portion in Nelson Township, while co-founder Benjamin Fairchild, referred to in early Kent County histories as the "other father" of Cedar Springs, owned and platted the western side in Solon Township.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-everett1878-6) Together, Hill and Fairchild drained the surrounding cedar swamp and offered alternate village lots free of charge to newcomers willing to build on them, helping transform the remote outpost into a lumber and shingle-milling center.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-everett1878-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-cityhistory-7)

### Railroad development and village incorporation
[edit]
Growth accelerated in 1868 when the Grand Rapids and Indiana Railroad constructed a railway line through the community.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-cityhistory-7) Fairchild also actively promoted competing rail connections, serving as a director for the Muskegon and Greenville Railroad in 1870, an effort that early county historians noted ultimately cost him his personal fortune.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-everett1878-6)
In March 1871, the Michigan Legislature officially incorporated Cedar Springs as a village.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-cityhistory-7) The village's first charter election was held at Fairchild's residence on April 2, 1871, where voters elected him as Cedar Springs' first village president.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-everett1878-6)

### 20th century and Red Flannel heritage
[edit]
During its timber era, local merchants supplied red flannel undergarments to lumberjacks working through Michigan winters.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-cityhistory2-8) In 1936, amid the Great Depression, a New York newspaper writer remarked that red flannel underwear was no longer available in the United States; editors Grace Hamilton and Nina Babcock of the local _Cedar Springs Clipper_ responded in print that town merchant Jack Pollock had plenty of red flannels in stock.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-rffhistory2-9) Picked up by the Associated Press, the story sparked a wave of mail orders from across the country and abroad; ultimately bringing tens of thousands of orders to local merchants and helping sustain the village's economy through the final years of the Depression.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-rffhistory2-9)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-cityhistory2-8) To celebrate the publicity and resulting economic boost, residents held the first annual Red Flannel Day on November 11, 1939, cementing Cedar Springs' nickname as "The Red Flannel Town".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-rffhistory2-9) The Red Flannel Festival is held on the first Saturday of October to this very day.
In October 1959, Cedar Springs incorporated as a city, driven largely by the need to establish independent water distribution and sanitary sewer systems rather than remaining divided between the taxing jurisdictions of Nelson and Solon townships.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Springs,_Michigan#cite_note-cityhistory-7)

Before the highways, the bustling downtown, and the craft breweries, the heart of Kent County was just a quiet trading post along a rushing river.
If you go back to the early 19th century, the land we now call Kent County was a heavily forested stretch of wilderness along the roaring rapids of the Grand River.
Here is the story of how a small fur-trading post became the official heart and county seat of Kent County!
The Spark: 1826 to 1831
It all started in 1826 when a French-Canadian fur trader named Louis Campau established a trading post right on the east bank of the Grand River. Campau, widely considered the "father" of Grand Rapids, officially bought the land from the federal government and platted the first town map in 1831.
That very same year, the Michigan Territorial Legislature officially "set off" Kent County from neighboring Kalamazoo County.
Why is it called "Kent" County?

# Michigan History | Before the highways, the bustling downtown, and the craft breweries, the heart of Kent County was just a quiet trading post along a rushing river | Facebook
The county was named after James Kent, a famous New York jurist and legal scholar. Why a New Yorker? Michigan actually hired him to defend its territorial rights against Ohio during the boundary dispute known as the "Toledo War." (Spoiler alert: We lost the strip but got the Upper Peninsula out of the deal—not a bad trade! )
Becoming the County Seat: 1836
While Kent County was created in 1831, it wasn’t fully "organized" with its own local government until 1836. Because of its ideal location along the river and its rapidly growing population, Grand Rapids was officially designated as the county seat.
1838: Grand Rapids officially incorporated as a village.
1850: With a population of just under 2,700 people, it officially became a city.
The Boom into "Furniture City"
With the county seat locked in, Grand Rapids exploded during the second half of the 19th century. The Grand River wasn't just beautiful—it was a highway for logs. Local sawmills processed giant Michigan pines, fueling a massive manufacturing boom that turned Grand Rapids into the "Furniture City" of the world.
Today, Kent County is the fourth-most populous county in Michigan, and Grand Rapids remains its proud, historic, and thriving center!

*   Grand River, flows through the county from its eastern border to the west, and after passing through Ottawa County, empties into Lake Michigan at Grand Haven. It has three tributaries in Kent County, listed in order of convergence:  
*   Flat River, enters the county from the east, and joins the Grand from the north, in Lowell.  
*   Thornapple River, enters the county from the south, and joins the Grand in Ada.  
*   Rogue River, enters the county from the north, and joins the Grand in Belmont.
These hiking and biking trails run through the county:
*   North Country Trail, runs north–south the length of the county, passing through Cedar Springs, Grattan and Lowell. Lowell is the trail's half-way point, and the national headquarters of the North Country Trail Association is located here.  
*   Thornapple Trail, begins in Kentwood and runs southeast through Dutton and Caledonia.  
*   White Pine Trail begins in Comstock Park and runs northeast through Belmont, Rockford, Cedar Springs, and Sand Lake.  
*   Kent Trails (which is singular in spite of the 's') runs north–south from John Ball Park in Grand Rapids to 84th Street in Byron Township, with an extension that runs east/west along 76th Street and north–south from 76th Street to Douglas Walker Park on 84th street.  
*   The Frederik Meijer Trail, which, as of November 2008, was incomplete, runs east/west mostly along the M-6 freeway and will connect the Kent Trails and the Thornapple Trail when completed.  
*   Cannon Township Trail runs through Cannon Township in the eastern part of the county from Cannon Township Center on M-44. It runs along M-44 then south near Sunfish Lake Road, turning east through the Cannonsburg Cemetery, and ends at Warren Townsend Park near Cannonsburg.

*   Thornapple River, enters the county from the south, and joins the Grand in Ada.  
*   Rogue River, enters the county from the north, and joins the Grand in Belmont.

History of Kent County and Grand Rapids, MI

Before the highways, the bustling downtown, and the craft breweries, the heart of Kent County was just a quiet trading post along a rushing river.
If you go back to the early 19th century, the land we now call Kent County was a heavily forested stretch of wilderness along the roaring rapids of the Grand River.
Here is the story of how a small fur-trading post became the official heart and county seat of Kent County!
The Spark: 1826 to 1831
It all started in 1826 when a French-Canadian fur trader named Louis Campau established a trading post right on the east bank of the Grand River. Campau, widely considered the "father" of Grand Rapids, officially bought the land from the federal government and platted the first town map in 1831.
That very same year, the Michigan Territorial Legislature officially "set off" Kent County from neighboring Kalamazoo County.
Why is it called "Kent" County?

# Michigan History | Before the highways, the bustling downtown, and the craft breweries, the heart of Kent County was just a quiet trading post along a rushing river | Facebook
The county was named after James Kent, a famous New York jurist and legal scholar. Why a New Yorker? Michigan actually hired him to defend its territorial rights against Ohio during the boundary dispute known as the "Toledo War." (Spoiler alert: We lost the strip but got the Upper Peninsula out of the deal—not a bad trade! )
Becoming the County Seat: 1836
While Kent County was created in 1831, it wasn’t fully "organized" with its own local government until 1836. Because of its ideal location along the river and its rapidly growing population, Grand Rapids was officially designated as the county seat.
1838: Grand Rapids officially incorporated as a village.
1850: With a population of just under 2,700 people, it officially became a city.
The Boom into "Furniture City"
With the county seat locked in, Grand Rapids exploded during the second half of the 19th century. The Grand River wasn't just beautiful—it was a highway for logs. Local sawmills processed giant Michigan pines, fueling a massive manufacturing boom that turned Grand Rapids into the "Furniture City" of the world.
Today, Kent County is the fourth-most populous county in Michigan, and Grand Rapids remains its proud, historic, and thriving center!
